content: The following individuals contributed significantly to the development of the guidelines: Matthias Egger from the University of Berne, Switzerland, and Christophe Fraser, Timothy Hallett, and Peter Vickerman from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, United Kingdom, respectively, provided expertise in epidemiological modeling and analysis. Daniel Keebler from the South African DST/NRF Centre of Excellence in Epidemiological Modeling and Analysis (SACEMA) at Stellenbosch University, South Africa, and Nicolas Menzies from the Harvard School of Public Health, USA, contributed to the modeling and public health aspects. Paul Revill from the University of York, United Kingdom, and Michael Schomaker from the University of Cape Town, South Africa, provided economic and statistical insights. John Stover from the Futures Institute, USA, contributed to programmatic modeling. Acknowledgments were extended to community representatives and organizations, including Alice Kate Armstrong and Florence Ngobeni from the Children’s HIV Association in South Africa, Laura Ferguson from the University of Southern California, USA, and Adam Garner and Amy Hsieh from the Global Network of People Living with HIV, USA. Carolyn Green, Nick Keeble, Gitau Mburu, and Mala Ram from the International HIV/AIDS Alliance, United Kingdom, also played key roles in community consultation efforts. WHO staff and consultants, including Andrew Ball and Philippa Easterbrook from the Department of HIV, coordinated the overall guideline development process. Cadi Irvine, a consultant, provided additional support. Meg Doherty supervised the clinical and service delivery components, while Eyusalem Kebede Negussie, Lulu Muhe, Nathan Shaffer, Marco Vitoria, and Joseph Perriëns facilitated the guideline development workstreams. Special thanks were given to WHO consultants Jhoney Barcarolo, Shaffiq Essajee, Martina Penazzato, and Amitabh Suthar for their contributions to writing and research. Ian Grubb provided overarching writing support, and David Breuer edited the text. The guidelines emphasize the use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for treating and preventing HIV infection. They recommend earlier initiation of ART, with a CD4 threshold of 500 cells/mm³ or less for adults, adolescents, and older children. Priority is given to individuals with advanced HIV disease or a CD4 count of 350 cells/mm³ or less. ART is recommended regardless of CD4 count for specific populations, including those with active tuberculosis, severe chronic liver disease due to hepatitis B, serodiscordant couples, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and children under five years of age. The guidelines advocate for harmonization of ART regimens across age groups and populations, with a preferred first-line regimen. Viral load testing is recommended as the preferred method for monitoring ART success and diagnosing treatment failure. The guidelines also promote community-based HIV testing and counseling, as well as testing for adolescents. Operational guidance focuses on improving retention in care, adherence to ART, and decentralizing ART provision to primary care, maternal and child health clinics, tuberculosis clinics, and drug dependence services. It addresses the implications of new clinical recommendations for laboratory services and supply systems. The guidelines reflect advances in HIV responses, including simplified, safer, and more affordable ART regimens, earlier initiation of treatment, and integration of HIV services with other health services. They aim to save lives, improve clinical outcomes, and reduce HIV incidence while addressing challenges for policymakers and implementers. Funding for the guidelines was provided by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), UNAIDS, and the United States Agency for International Development. WHO also acknowledged the contributions of institutions that provided staff time and in-kind support. Dr. Margaret Chan, Director-General of WHO, emphasized the importance of these guidelines in accelerating progress in the global HIV response. She encouraged countries and development partners to seize this opportunity to push the HIV epidemic into irreversible decline.
